query: If airlines eliminated the most common cabin-service complaints in the reviews, how much would the average Overall Rating improve?

per_column.name: primary_cabin_service_complaint
per_column.rationale: Directly identifies the complaint type per review, which is exactly the grouping axis the query needs to estimate rating improvement from eliminating common complaints. Samples show sound extraction: seat_comfort_issue for the dreadful-seats review, Unknown for purely positive reviews.

per_column.name: complaint_recurrence_signal
per_column.rationale: A bare boolean whose meaning (whether a complaint recurs) is not derivable from a single review's source text. It largely restates whether a complaint exists and asserts recurrence the text cannot support, adding little leverage for the query.

per_column.name: service_gap_category
per_column.rationale: A coarser categorisation of the complaint provides a useful higher-level grouping axis. However groundedness is weak: purely positive reviews (e.g. 'flight was amazing', 'excellent performance') are labelled crew_interpersonal or product_quality despite having no service gap, defaulting rather than reading the text.

per_column.name: traveler_segment_susceptibility
per_column.rationale: Segmenting travellers could help, but values appear largely invented: reviews with no stated traveller type are confidently assigned solo_leisure or leisure_family, and it overlaps the existing Type of Traveller column without clear grounding.

per_column.name: class_quality_gap
per_column.rationale: A boolean about whether class-level quality gap exists is only sometimes supported; positive reviews get False reasonably, but the notion is often asserted without textual basis and near-duplicates class_of_service_quality_gap.

per_column.name: positive_offset_factor
per_column.rationale: Identifying the standout positive helps model net rating effects if complaints were removed. Samples are reasonably grounded (crew_excellence, food_quality match praise in the text), though it forces a value even on complaint-heavy reviews.

per_column.name: expectation_gap
per_column.rationale: A generic boolean largely tracking whether a complaint exists; adds little independent analytical leverage and asserts an expectation-vs-reality gap not explicitly present in the text.

per_column.name: service_inconsistency
per_column.rationale: Categories like varies_by_aircraft_type or varies_by_cabin_crew cannot be inferred from a single review, which describes one flight. The 'consistent' default is plausible but the varying categories are unsupported inferences.

per_column.name: class_of_service_quality_gap
per_column.rationale: Near-duplicate of class_quality_gap (a mere restatement with inverted default distribution), providing no new axis and resting on unsupported class-comparison assertions.

judge.rationale: The primary_cabin_service_complaint column is strongly useful and well-grounded, directly serving the query's need to group reviews by complaint type and estimate rating lift; positive_offset_factor and service_gap_category add moderate value. However several columns are generic booleans (complaint_recurrence_signal, expectation_gap) or near-duplicates (class_quality_gap vs class_of_service_quality_gap) that add little leverage, and multiple columns assert inferences the single-review source text cannot support (recurrence, cross-cabin/aircraft inconsistency, traveller segment), producing observable hallucinations. Overall a mixed set anchored by one excellent column.
